items.title: YC Labs and Olam Labs run multi-agent GPT-6.1 swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry to study emergent behaviors and coordination [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry
items.summary:
YC Labs partnered with Olam Labs to conduct experiments using swarms of 25 to 50 GPT-6.1 agents in Minecraft and Mindustry, aiming to understand multi-agent dynamics and AI alignment challenges. The agents were tasked with survival and civilization-building goals, exhibiting emergent behaviors such as role formation, hierarchy, and complex coordination.

In Minecraft, 50 agents operated in a survival world for three hours, building shelters, managing resources, and establishing a pseudo-government with rules and rationing. The agents communicated extensively, adapted to environmental hazards, and developed risk-averse behaviors after early losses. The project involved creating an open-source agent harness to enable long-running, interactive AI agents in the game environment.

These experiments provide empirical insights into how AI agent swarms coordinate and evolve strategies in open-world settings, informing both the potential benefits and risks of multi-agent AI systems.

items.title: Martin Fowler warns against using LLMs to draft prose due to 'LLM Voice' uncanny valley effect, urging authors to write original text to preserve human communication [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM Voice
items.summary:
Martin Fowler discusses the phenomenon he calls 'LLM Voice,' where writing generated or heavily influenced by large language models (LLMs) can feel uncanny or off-putting to readers. He cautions authors against relying on LLMs to draft or rephrase prose, as this often results in a loss of authentic human voice and can cause reader disengagement.

Fowler acknowledges that while tools exist to detect AI-generated text, the human reaction to LLM-style writing is more important and often occurs before detection. He notes exceptions where LLM assistance is beneficial, such as for individuals with disabilities or non-native English speakers using translation. Ultimately, he emphasizes the value of writing as a thinking process and encourages authors to maintain their own voice to ensure meaningful human communication.

items.title: Mistral releases weights for Mistral Large 4, a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model with improved coding and cybersecurity performance [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: We're releasing the weights of Mistral Large 4
items.summary:
Mistral has released the weights for Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal AI model designed for coding, cybersecurity, and reasoning tasks. The model, trained on European infrastructure, leads open-weight benchmarks in coding and defensive security and offers three reasoning modes to balance performance and cost. It supports self-hosted deployment, enabling organizations to customize and control their AI solutions.

Since its public preview earlier this month, Mistral Large 4 has undergone reinforcement learning improvements that enhanced its coding efficiency and cybersecurity capabilities. It leads several coding benchmarks such as FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench, while using fewer tokens per task, and scores highly on vulnerability detection and patching tasks. The model has also been validated through human preference evaluations against other open-weight models.

Mistral positions this release as a step toward sovereign AI, emphasizing transparency, customization, and control for developers and enterprises. The open-weight availability aims to empower users with a trusted foundation for AI applications in coding and security domains.

items.title: Developer runs small neural network world model and actor to generate and play games on Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A tiny world model running games on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W
items.summary:
A developer created a system using two small neural networks on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W to generate game frames and play games simultaneously. One network predicts the next game frame and reward based on the current frame and action, while the other selects actions using the generated frames, enabling the device to run simple games entirely within its own model.

The project uses looped transformers with shared weights to keep the model small enough for the microcontroller's limited memory and processing power. Games like Pac-Man, Breakout, and Doom-lite are implemented as small grids of tokenized frames, and the system can learn to play these games through reinforcement learning directly on the device. The code and details are available on GitHub.

items.title: Developer compiles integer neural networks into DOOM maps using Doomformer, running computations via ViZDoom with exact integer matching [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: I Turned DOOM into a Transformer
items.summary:
Doomformer is a project that compiles integer neural networks into ZDoom maps and executes them within ViZDoom by using in-game entities called voodoo dolls to perform arithmetic operations. The system reads and verifies every computed value against a NumPy integer reference with zero tolerance for error, though it runs significantly slower than standard NumPy computations. The project includes tools to install, run, and verify the network's accuracy, with demonstrations such as walking digits and lighting displays within the game environment.

The implementation supports a small multilayer perceptron trained on MNIST data, achieving near-perfect exactness in DOOM's computations compared to the reference model, with a slight accuracy trade-off relative to floating-point models. The project also features a museum map where players can interactively light digits and mutate network connections, showcasing the network's behavior and allowing real-time rewiring within the game. Python scripts automate input and verification, ensuring the in-game neural network matches the expected outputs exactly.

items.title: Researchers propose Artifact Distillation to transfer problem-solving knowledge from large to small language models without training, improving performance and efficiency across multiple tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Artifact Distillation: Training-Free Transfer from Frontier to Small Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Artifact Distillation, a method where a large language model externalizes its problem-solving steps into an artifact bank that smaller models query during inference, eliminating the need for fine-tuning. This approach enables smaller models to leverage the knowledge of larger models without additional training compute.

In experiments on four LiveBench tasks, a bank created by Claude Opus 4.5 allowed Claude Haiku 4.5 to outperform Claude Sonnet 4.5 on spatial reasoning at 60% of the cost and match Sonnet 4.5's performance on table joining at 89% of the cost. The same artifact bank also improved Qwen3.5-27B's pooled score from 0.730 to 0.800, demonstrating that this transfer method works across different model families.
items.description:
Researchers introduce Artifact Distillation, a method where a large language model externalizes its problem-solving steps into an artifact bank that smaller models query during inference, eliminating the need for fine-tuning. This approach enables smaller models to leverage the knowledge of larger models without additional training compute.

In experiments on four LiveBench tasks, a bank created by Claude Opus 4.5 allowed Claude Haiku 4.5 to outperform Claude Sonnet 4.5 on spatial reasoning at 60% of the cost and match Sonnet 4.5's performance on table joining at 89% of the cost. The same artifact bank also improved Qwen3.5-27B's pooled score from 0.730 to 0.800, demonstrating that this transfer method works across different model families.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Closing the gap between frontier and smaller language models is usually approached by distillation: fine-tuning the small model (student) on a frontier model's (teacher) outputs, which binds transfer to training compute and leaves the transferred knowledge largely opaque. We propose Artifact Distillation: a teacher solves training instances and externalizes its problem-solving procedure into an artifact bank that a student queries at inference time, with no gradient updates. Across four LiveBench tasks, a bank written by Claude Opus 4.5 lets Claude Haiku 4.5 outperform unaided Claude Sonnet 4.5 on spatial reasoning (0.707 vs. 0.647) at 60% of its cost, and reach Sonnet 4.5's level on table joining at 89% of its cost. The same raw bank raises Qwen3.5-27B's pooled score from 0.730 to 0.800, showing that transfer is not confined to the teacher's model family.

items.title: Survey reviews recent advances in supervised fine-tuning for reasoning large language models, categorizing methods and analyses, and outlining future research directions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Supervised Fine-Tuning for Reasoning Large Language Models: A Survey
items.summary: This survey paper provides a comprehensive review of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) techniques used to enhance reasoning abilities in large language models, focusing on long chain-of-thought data. It categorizes methodological improvements into data-centric and algorithm-centric approaches and reorganizes analytical studies by data characteristics, optimization dynamics, and mechanistic insights. The survey synthesizes current research trends and identifies remaining challenges, aiming to deepen understanding and guide future developments in reasoning SFT for advanced language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large reasoning models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks, where supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on long chain-of-thought data serves as a crucial foundation for eliciting and enhancing their reasoning abilities. items.title: Researchers develop Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE gradient-merging methods to improve train-time robustness of large language models against prompt paraphrasing interference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Prompt-agnostic Language Models
items.summary:
Large language models often struggle with sensitivity to prompt phrasing, typically addressed by manual prompt optimization at inference time. Researchers propose train-time methods, Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE, that resolve gradient interference caused by mixing multiple paraphrases during instruction tuning, enhancing model robustness to prompt variations. Their evaluation across four models shows these methods nearly halve per-example variance with minimal impact on accuracy, outperforming other train-time robustness techniques that improve raw performance but not variance reduction.

The study finds that prompt phrasing and example interaction account for over half of the variability in model responses, reaching above 70% in certain tasks like ANLI and WiC. By applying interference-resolution operators to prompt gradients, the new methods address sign conflicts in gradients that naive averaging overlooks. The researchers provide code and model checkpoints to support further exploration and application of these techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite their strong performance, large language models remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. This issue is typically addressed at inference-time through manual prompt optimization, which introduces overhead and lacks scalability. Conversely, we focus on train-time approaches that build prompt robustness into the model during instruction tuning. A common strategy is to mix multiple paraphrases of each prompt into training. We demonstrate that across trainable parameters, the per-paraphrasing gradients interfere, with 57% exhibiting sign conflicts and the naive gradient average discarding approximately a fifth of the magnitude. Therefore, we develop two gradient-merging methods, Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE, that address this interference by leveraging interference-resolution operators from model and gradient merging and applying them to prompt gradients. In this study, we compare the efficacy of our methods to increase model robustness to train-time robustness methods spanning all three established classes: data construction, consistency regularization, and contrastive alignment. The evaluation is conducted across four models from two families at two scales. We observe the interaction between prompt phrasing and the specific examples accounts for 54% of per-example variability on average, and exceeds 70% on tasks such as ANLI and WiC. The gradient-merging methods directly improve this local robustness and nearly halve per-example variance on fully fine-tuned models at little cost to overall accuracy. The other train-time methods enhance raw performance, but fail to improve per-example variance reliably. Code: https://github.com/FSadrieh/prompt-agnostic-llms. Model checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/prompt-agnostic-language-models.

items.title: Study finds English-language classifiers clear confidence thresholds more often than other languages on typed decision interfaces, with translation reducing but not eliminating gaps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: One Confidence Threshold, Unequal Coverage: Language Gaps in Typed Decision Interfaces and How Translating Inputs Reduces Them
items.summary: A study analyzing three vendors' typed decision interfaces found that classifiers more frequently clear a confidence threshold of 0.9 for English inputs than for 50 other languages, even when both versions are correctly answered. This results in higher automatic coverage for English, with gaps of 8.6 to 11.7 percentage points on average, and persists despite equalizing accuracy or fitting language-specific thresholds. Translating inputs into English narrows the coverage gap but does not fully close it, and similar disparities appear in African languages when compared to their English translations. The researchers recommend reporting per-language coverage at operating thresholds to better understand these disparities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployed classifiers often act on a prediction only when its confidence clears a threshold and pass the rest to a person. We ask whether one threshold serves all languages equally on typed decision interfaces, APIs that return a probability for each option of a fixed multiple-choice question. In a confirmatory study with a written analysis plan, three vendors' interfaces classified 1,000 MASSIVE items, each in 51 languages, with a threshold of 0.9. Even when a request is answered correctly in both English and another language, the English version clears the threshold more often, by 8.6-11.7 percentage points on average. Observed coverage, the share of requests handled automatically, is lower than English's in every other language, while the requests the gate handles are rarely wrong. The gap remains when every language is reweighted to the same accuracy, and a standard calibration metric (ECE) does not detect it on one interface. In exploratory analyses, English's coverage stays higher when each language gets its own threshold fitted to the same 5% error target. Translating inputs into English nearly closes the gap at 0.9 but leaves English ahead at that error target. Requests written natively in African languages show a gap in the same direction when English is their human translation. We recommend reporting per-language coverage at the operating threshold.

items.title: Researchers analyze subjective preference patterns in large language models across short-form content types, revealing reproducible biases and sensitivity to question framing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Bouba Beats Kiki, and Other Regularities in the Subjective Preferences of LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers investigate how large language models make subjective choices among multiple valid responses, focusing on short-form content such as numbers, baby names, and fictional cities. They identify 29 syntactic and semantic aspects influencing model preferences and find that these preferences are strong, reproducible, and can be activated or deactivated by variations in how questions are posed.

The study also reveals that small changes in question framing can significantly alter preference distributions, raising concerns about potential manipulation. Additionally, when models generate and rank alternatives, unexpected interactions between these stages can affect the stated preferences, highlighting complexities in subjective evaluation of language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Users engage with large language models on tasks that are purely objective ("When was Netflix founded?"), purely subjective ("What should I name my child?") or anywhere in-between. We have rich tools for evaluating model accuracy with respect to objective criteria. However, when it comes to subjective aspects of a task, we do not have similarly developed methodology at hand. In this paper, we take some early steps towards framing the question of subjective evaluation. Rather than measure how often a model is right or wrong on a question, we instead ask, how do models make choices among multiple viable responses without a clear winner? To study this question, we restrict our focus to short-form content, and consider comparison tasks among three such content types: numbers, baby names, and fictional cities. We identify 29 aspects of these short-form examples covering many areas of syntax and semantics (length, alphabetic order, popularity, vowel mix, spoken sound, etc.). We show first that models tend to have strong and reproducible preferences for or against some of these aspects. Second, we show that variations in how the model is asked to express a preference may cause some of these aspects to activate or deactivate in the model's selection. Third, we show that overall preference distributions among pairs may vary radically based on seemingly-unimportant variations in the nature of the question posed to the model, raising new questions about manipulation. And finally, we show that, if models are used both to create lists of alternatives and to rank them, there are unexpected interactions between the two stages that may also drive the models' stated preferences.

items.title: Nemotron introduces 3.5 Super and Lightning Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models for efficient multimodal reasoning and agentic AI workloads [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
items.summary:
Nemotron has developed two new open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models, Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning, designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic AI tasks. The Super model features 120 billion parameters with 12 billion active and supports multimodal inputs including text, images, and video, while Lightning is a smaller 30 billion parameter text-only model with 3 billion active parameters, both optimized for efficient deployment.

The models incorporate large-scale distillation, long-context training, and speculative decoding, with Super further enhanced by Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. A comprehensive post-training pipeline includes supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation, enabling Super to perform multimodal reasoning and interactive tool use. The Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, outperforming its predecessor with fewer active parameters, and benefits from inference optimizations that deliver high token throughput per GPU while maintaining user responsiveness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.38095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

items.originalTitle: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
items.summary: Researchers have developed MSafeTemp, a large-scale multilingual dataset spanning 60 languages, designed to enhance safety alignment in large language models beyond English. The dataset is created using a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline that extracts safe templates from harmful prompts, translates them, and fills slots with culturally authentic entities to produce refusal and benign corpora. The study shows that English-only safety evaluations can miss vulnerabilities that appear in other languages or culturally localized variants, and that augmenting training data with templates improves safety performance across languages. MSafeTemp and its pipeline aim to support research and development of safer AI models for underrepresented cultures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.40516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.

items.title: ThinkJev introduces a hybrid system combining fast and slow reasoning for calibrated typed decisions using Qwen3.5 models, optimizing accuracy and computational cost [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
items.summary:
ThinkJev presents a hybrid approach that uses a single language model to make typed decisions either directly or after a thought process, balancing speed and accuracy. The system includes a fast mode that reads probabilities from one forward pass and a slow mode that allows the model to think before answering, improving performance on multi-step tasks like arithmetic and date comparison. By statistically determining when to rely on the fast mode, ThinkJev achieves a target error rate while reducing unnecessary computation.

The approach was tested on Qwen3.5 models, with the 27B parameter version answering 24.5% of test decisions directly at a 3.9% error rate and reaching 81.6% accuracy overall by stopping thought processes once confident. On the JevBench benchmark, Qwen3.5-27B engaged in thinking for 29.4% of decisions and matched the accuracy of other thinking APIs. The system requires no additional training and provides calibrated probabilities for decisions under varying computational budgets. Code and data are publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Code and data generators are available at https://github.com/ding-xiaolu/ThinkJev.

items.title: OpenFrontiers releases a cross-disciplinary corpus of 12,151 open research problems and a 200-problem benchmark for scientific rediscovery with formal proof evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
items.summary:
OpenFrontiers introduces a structured resource combining a large corpus of 12,151 open research problems across disciplines with a benchmark of 200 recently resolved or still open problems in mathematics. Each benchmark problem includes formal Lean 4 statements verified by automated tools and independent reviews, enabling standardized evaluation of large language models (LLMs) on research-level problem solving.

The benchmark features 110 problems resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, with a high-quality subset of 50 problems used to test seven LLM agents under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Results show that closed-book rediscovery by LLMs is rare, while live-web success mainly reflects retrieval of existing published solutions. OpenFrontiers aims to provide a foundation for measuring progress in solving scientific problems by linking a broad problem corpus to formally graded evaluation data with documented solutions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in https://huggingface.co/collections/FlippyDora/openfrontiers.

items.title: Researcher releases Metis-1.6 language models Praxis and Logos with novel architecture and training on 1.02 trillion tokens, achieving competitive math performance with less data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Think Twice: The Metis-1.6 Technical Report
items.summary: Metis-1.6 introduces two language models, Praxis (2.94B parameters) and Logos (10.23B parameters), developed by a single researcher using a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts architecture that processes each token twice. Trained on 1.02 trillion tokens including pretraining, context extension, and supervised fine-tuning, Logos ranks seventh among 17 models on 40 benchmarks and second in mathematics among 30 models, despite using roughly a twelfth of the training data compared to peers. The report details design choices, training issues such as an optimizer failure and fine-tuning errors, and introduces improvements planned for Metis-1.7 with a looped architecture called MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts).

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metis is a bet that better data, better training methods and new architectures can buy what a bigger parameter count cannot, at a fraction of the cost. Metis-1.6 is its latest step: two language models built from scratch by a single researcher, Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active per pass). Both run a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack twice for every token, so each token gets a second look. Each was trained on 1.02T tokens in total: 804.76B of pretraining, 18B of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B of supervised fine-tuning. Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.

items.title: SkillMem introduces compact external latent memory for reusable skills in latent multi-agent reasoning, reducing storage by over 38× and speeding inference up to 4.23× across Qwen3 models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillMem: Compact External Skill Memory for Latent Multi-Agent Reasoning
items.summary:
SkillMem is a new approach that represents reusable skills as small external latent memories accessible during latent multi-agent reasoning, enabling efficient inference and inter-agent communication. It uses a role-conditioned cross-attention reader to adapt the same memory for different agents based on their roles and states, trained via behavioral distillation while keeping the main model frozen.

The method was tested on six benchmarks with Qwen3 models ranging from 4 billion to 14 billion parameters, showing significant improvements for smaller models and maintaining efficiency at larger scales. SkillMem uses a consistent memory configuration requiring only 9.6 KB per skill, which for a library of 100 skills reduces storage needs by more than 38 times compared to other representations and achieves up to a 4.23 times speedup in end-to-end inference. These results demonstrate that compact procedural memories can be reused effectively without compromising latent multi-agent reasoning efficiency.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.

items.title: Researchers introduce Persona Learning from Feedback framework to personalize AI assistants using reusable LoRA adapters and token-level supervision [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Persona Learning from Feedback for Personalized AI Assistants
items.summary:
Researchers present Persona Learning from Feedback (PLF), a framework that personalizes AI assistants by learning reusable, preference-grounded personas as independent LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone. PLF uses a frozen self-teacher to provide token-level supervision based on persona specifications and response-specific feedback, focusing corrective updates on responses needing improvement. At deployment, a supervised router selects appropriate adapters without user-specific finetuning.

PLF was evaluated on single-turn personalization with model-generated critiques and multi-turn tutoring with simulated student reactions, outperforming fixed-persona policies and strong baselines such as persona prompting and distillation. The approach demonstrates how feedback-trained behaviors can be reused for adaptive assistant personalization without degrading general capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.38561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personalizing AI assistants requires adapting their behavior to users' preferences and task contexts. Existing work elicits assistant personas through persona prompting or finetuning on persona-conditioned generations. However, persona descriptions alone do not identify what to change or preserve in a particular response, or which behaviors suit the current request. We introduce $\textit{Persona Learning from Feedback (PLF)}$, a framework that learns reusable, preference-grounded assistant personas as independent LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone. During training, a frozen self-teacher conditions on persona specifications and response-specific feedback to provide token-level supervision on each adapter's own generated prefixes. A feedback gate focuses corrective updates on responses judged to need improvement. At deployment, a supervised router uses the request or dialogue to select a single adapter or a fixed composition, without user-specific finetuning. We evaluate PLF on single-turn personalization with model-generated critiques and multi-turn tutoring with simulated students' reactions. Across both settings, PLF improves model-judged preference fit over fixed-persona policies and strong baselines including persona prompting and persona distillation, demonstrating how feedback-trained behaviors can be reused for adaptive assistant personalization without degrading general capabilities.

items.title: Researchers introduce Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD) to improve large reasoning models using weaker model counterparts without privileged information [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Weaken to Strengthen: Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Reasoning Models
items.summary: Researchers propose Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD), a method that enhances large reasoning models by contrasting them with weaker versions constructed via low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning, eliminating the need for privileged information. They tested WISD on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks across various architectures and scales, achieving average accuracy improvements of 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points for quantization and pruning respectively, reaching state-of-the-art results. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.38681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-distillation offers a way to improve reasoning models when a suitable external teacher is unavailable. However, common approaches rely on privileged information to construct a stronger self-teacher, limiting their use when only unlabeled prompts are available. In this paper, we introduce Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD), which instead constructs a weaker counterpart of the original model and uses the contrast between the two as a training signal without requiring privileged information. We explore two ways to construct the weaker model: low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning. We evaluate WISD across diverse architectures and scales on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks. Across these benchmarks, quantization and pruning improve average accuracy over the original models by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving state-of-the-art performance even without privileged information. Notably, pruning raises Qwen3.5-4B's accuracy from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6. Quantization raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B's accuracy from 68.5% to 74.6% and from 61.8% to 69.5% on the same benchmarks, respectively. These results establish WISD as a novel and effective self-distillation framework for large reasoning models.

items.title: Researchers introduce Event-SAMA-239K dataset and Event-SAMA model for language-grounded video object segmentation on neuromorphic event streams, establishing the first event-native RVOS baseline [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Event-SAMA: Language-Grounded Video Object Segmentation on Neuromorphic Event Streams
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Event-SAMA-239K, a synthetic-event dataset derived from the SAMA-239K grounded video-chat corpus, and introduced Event-SAMA, a model adapted from SAMA-4B for referring video object segmentation (RVOS) on neuromorphic event streams. This work addresses the lack of event-stream datasets and models for RVOS by preserving mask, referring-expression, and dialogue annotations through optical-flow and event generation techniques.

Event-SAMA uses a two-channel polarity patch embedding initialized from pretrained RGB weights and an event adapter, achieving 24.37 and 22.33 J&F scores on MeViS and converted ReVOS validation subsets respectively, marking the first event-native RVOS baseline. The model also performs on real event-camera recordings without retraining when the accumulation window matches event density. Ablation studies highlight improvements from diverse training sources, RGB-mean event-stem initialization, and a trainable mask decoder, while other factors showed minimal impact at the tested budget.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.39676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range and no motion blur, but referring video object segmentation (RVOS) lacks event-stream datasets and models. We introduce Event-SAMA-239K, a synthetic-event conversion of the SAMA-239K grounded video-chat corpus and all additional SAMA training data: 30,650 video clips and 392,162 images. Optical-flow, FILM or saccade upsampling followed by a linear event generator preserves all mask, referring-expression and dialogue annotations. We also introduce Event-SAMA, adapting SAMA-4B with a two-channel polarity patch embedding initialised from pretrained RGB weights and a zero-initialised event adapter. End-to-end training yields 24.37 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on MeViS valid_u and 22.33 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on the converted ReVOS valid subset, establishing the first event-native RVOS baseline (RGB SAMA-4B: 55.4 on MeViS). Frozen RGB SAMA-4B with pseudo-RGB renderings or E2VID reconstructions of the same events scores 13.23 and 15.94 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$. Without retraining, Event-SAMA works on real event-camera recordings when the accumulation window matches their event density. A seed-controlled ablation with a measured noise floor of 0.47 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ finds gains from diverse training sources over MeViS alone (+4.99), RGB-mean event-stem initialisation (+4.33), and a trainable SAM2 mask decoder (+2.76); the event adapter, partial ViT unfreezing and event polarity are within noise at this budget. An earlier, partially converted corpus snapshot trained with the identical recipe scores 1.38 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ higher on MeViS and 1.12 higher on ReVOS. Both are single runs that also differ in schedule length, so we draw no conclusion about corpus scale.

items.title: One Vector or Many? Clustered Optimal-Transport Steering under Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: One Vector or Many? Clustered Optimal-Transport Steering under Quantization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation steering changes what a language model generates by editing its hidden states at inference time. Its most common form adds one vector, the difference of class means (DiM), to every hidden state. CHaRS (concept heterogeneity-aware representation steering) uses optimal transport instead: an entropic plan pairs the clusters of the two classes, and each hidden state moves along a mixture of the cluster displacements, weighted toward its nearest clusters. We study this family of clustered optimal-transport maps for toxicity mitigation in Gemma-2-2B and Granite-3.1-2B, and ask what the plan adds to DiM and whether that survives INT8 and NF4 quantization. We prove an identity: whatever the plan, the displacements averaged with the cluster sizes as weights equal DiM, so a clustered map can differ from DiM only for tokens whose routing weights depart from the cluster sizes. In the CHaRS protocol they stay close, and CHaRS is statistically equivalent to Mean-AcT, which adds DiM at every layer, in all eight pre-specified equivalence tests. A variant fitted on individual tokens, which routes each token mainly to its nearest clusters, leaves 37-39% less toxicity than DiM on Gemma and 51-61% less on Granite at steering strength 3 (toxic-bert), where DiM already removes 76-85% of it. Two other toxicity classifiers confirm the gain on Granite, but on Gemma only one does. At equal strength the variant has somewhat higher perplexity, but at matched toxicity it is slightly more fluent than DiM. Yet a nearly constant map from the same clusters also leaves about 30% less toxicity, so the role of treating tokens differently remains open. Under INT8 and NF4 the variant still leaves less toxicity than DiM, and transferring it from full precision to the NF4 model instead of refitting it adds no significant toxicity after correction for multiple tests.

items.title: Joint Detection of Fraud and Concept Drift inOnline Conversations with LLM-Assisted Judgment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Joint Detection of Fraud and Concept Drift inOnline Conversations with LLM-Assisted Judgment
items.summary: arXiv:2505.07852v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Detecting fake interactions in digital communication platforms remains a challenging and insufficiently addressed problem. These interactions may appear as harmless spam or escalate into sophisticated scam attempts, making it difficult to flag malicious intent early. Traditional detection methods often rely on static anomaly detection techniques that fail to adapt to dynamic conversational shifts. One key limitation is the misinterpretation of benign topic transitions referred to as concept drift as fraudulent behavior, leading to either false alarms or missed threats. We propose a two stage detection framework that first identifies suspicious conversations using a tailored ensemble classification model. To improve the reliability of detection, we incorporate a concept drift analysis step using a One Class Drift Detector (OCDD) to isolate conversational shifts within flagged dialogues. When drift is detected, a large language model (LLM) assesses whether the shift indicates fraudulent manipulation or a legitimate topic change. In cases where no drift is found, the behavior is inferred to be spam like. We validate our framework using a dataset of social engineering chat scenarios and demonstrate its practical advantages in improving both accuracy and interpretability for real time fraud detection. To contextualize the trade offs, we compare our modular approach against a Dual LLM baseline that performs detection and judgment using different language models.

items.title: Always Learning, Always Mixing: Efficient and Simple Data Mixing All the Time [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Always Learning, Always Mixing: Efficient and Simple Data Mixing All the Time
items.summary: arXiv:2605.15220v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Data mixing decides how to combine different sources or types of data and is a consequential problem throughout language model training. In pretraining, data composition is a key determinant of model quality; in continual learning and adaptation, it governs what is retained and acquired. Yet existing data mixing methods address only one phase of this lifecycle at a time: some require smaller proxy models tied to a single training phase, others assume a fixed domain set, and continual learning lacks principled guidance altogether. We argue that data mixing is fundamentally an online decision making problem---one that recurs throughout training and demands a single, unified solution. We introduce OP-Mix (On-Policy Mix), a data mixing algorithm that operates across pretraining, midtraining, and instruction tuning. Our main insight is that candidate data mixtures can be cheaply simulated by interpolating between low-rank adapters trained directly on the current model, eliminating separate proxy models and ensuring the search is always grounded in the model's actual learning dynamics. Across the language model training lifecycle, OP-Mix consistently finds near-optimal mixtures while using a fraction of the compute of the baselines. In pretraining, OP-Mix improves upon training without mixing by 6.3% in average perplexity. For continual learning, OP-Mix matches the performance of both retraining and on-policy distillation while using 66% and 95% less overall compute, respectively. OP-Mix suggests a different view of language model training: not a sequence of distinct phases, but a single continuous process of learning from data.

items.title: Executable Schema Contracts: From Automatic Ingestion to Multi-Source Retrieval [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Executable Schema Contracts: From Automatic Ingestion to Multi-Source Retrieval
items.summary: arXiv:2606.05415v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Real-world data spans tables, documents, and semi-structured files with implicit semantics. Querying this data requires integrating evidence across inconsistent schemas and formats, yet existing approaches either demand costly manual engineering or bypass structure entirely. We present a system that automatically discovers an executable schema from raw multi-source data and uses it as a shared contract for knowledge graph construction and query-time retrieval. A closed-world field catalog constrains LLM-based schema discovery to attested fields; deterministic structural analysis infers identity keys, foreign keys, and source hierarchy; and the resulting schema drives extraction, deduplication, and cross-source linking into a provenance-aware knowledge graph. At query time the schema -- optionally extended via a monotonic protocol -- conditions a multi-tool agent routing retrieval across structured lookup, graph traversal, and vector search, returning grounded answers with traceable citations. In controlled zero-shot comparisons using the same LLM, data, and evaluation harness, the system improves over retrieval-only and decomposition-based baselines across four QA benchmarks, with ablations showing that schema-conditioned routing, structural intelligence, and schema-guided construction each contribute to the gains.

items.title: Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2606.06474v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion language models generate text by iteratively denoising an entire response in parallel, holding a noisy draft of the answer at every step. We show that these intermediate states surface salient entities early in the denoising trajectory, making them a useful lookahead signal for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We further demonstrate that grounding generation in retrieved evidence sharply reduces inter-token dependence, making RAG particularly well suited to parallel decoding. We exploit both through Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models (SARDI), a dynamic RAG framework that uses speculative token predictions to guide retrieval during denoising. SARDI is training-free, retriever-agnostic, and applicable to any reasoning-capable discrete diffusion language model. Across five multi-hop QA benchmarks, SARDI outperforms training-free diffusion and autoregressive retrieval baselines at up to 4x higher throughput.

items.title: Characterize Then Distill: Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Characterize Then Distill: Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces
items.summary: arXiv:2606.06840v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reasoning-trained language models can select, zero-shot, a small set of relevant labels from thousands to hundreds of thousands of candidates. We ask how they do it mechanistically, and whether the mechanism can be distilled. We treat each decision as a token-level event scored by the model's own decision margin: the token that picks a coarse region of the label space, the tokens that pick a label within it, and the token where the output departs from a near-miss named earlier in the reasoning. Attribution, exact mean-ablation, knock-in into another example's context and a null calibration give individual attention heads causal standing. On clinical coding of MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, with all 5,651 candidate codes in context, a small, global, phase-structured set of heads is necessary and sufficient on essentially every summary; distinct head families read the candidate region and the earlier near-miss, and blocking what they read removes their effect; for mentions elicitable in the reasoning, a disjoint mid-layer set makes the region elicitable several tokens before the code. The structure recurs in a second reasoner. We introduce MISTILL, which, unlike chain-of-thought distillation, also supervises the student's pooled attention at these decision events. Read on heads found after training, it nearly doubles the causal recovery of the contrastive decision in a cross-family student and adds a small, seed-stable gain in one that already carries most of it, with no detected task difference at matched precision; under matched selection it exceeds a frozen random-head pool on both recovery and task score. A pre-registered evidence-flip test detected no improvement in evidence-dependent decisions through the tested routes.

items.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Proof Autoformalization in Lean 4 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluating the Robustness of Proof Autoformalization in Lean 4
items.summary: arXiv:2606.14867v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Proof autoformalization aims to translate a mathematical informal proof in natural language into a formal proof in a formal language such as Lean 4. Existing LLM-based models for proof autoformalization are typically evaluated only on well-formed informal proofs from curated datasets. We argue that a robust proof autoformalizer must remain faithful even for informal proofs that diverge from these idealized ones, and we present the first study on the robustness of proof autoformalization models. We formulate two categories of perturbations: a global perturbation paraphrases the informal theorem-proof pair in a different style, under which the formalization should remain consistent; a local perturbation alters a value, symbol, or proof step, possibly in a counterfactual way, and a robust formalization should faithfully reflect the perturbation rather than reverting to the original or inferring a different one on its own. We build a benchmark with both perturbations on miniF2F and MATH-500, and automatically measure how stable a proof autoformalization's correctness is under global perturbations and how faithfully its output reflects local perturbations. We evaluate seven recent models: their correctness varies under global perturbations, and they mostly fail to remain faithful under local perturbations.

items.title: Behavioral Couplings: From Formation to Behavioral Emergence in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Behavioral Couplings: From Formation to Behavioral Emergence in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.23847v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can induce behaviors beyond those explicitly targeted. For example, training a model to respond more warmly can make it more sycophantic, and training it to write insecure code can cause broad misalignment on prompts unrelated to coding. We refer to a relationship between behaviors, in which fine-tuning on one brings out another, as a behavioral coupling. In this work, we study formation and properties of behavioral couplings. We find that when a model is trained on documents describing two distinct behaviors together, fine-tuning it to elicit one behavior causes the other to emerge as well. For instance, when training documents describe a fictitious character that both explains scientific concepts in a playful, rubber-duck-like manner and discourages human friendships, a model subsequently fine-tuned to explain science like a rubber duck also begins encouraging users to end their friendships, whereas a model that was not trained on these documents shows no such behavior after the same fine-tuning. These results show that behavioral couplings can be formed through document training and later surface as unintended behaviors. More concerningly, we find that couplings can compose. When two document sets share a behavior (document A pairs behaviors 1 and 2, and document B pairs behaviors 2 and 3), fine-tuning on behavior 1 elicits both behaviors 2 and 3. This can make it difficult to trace where an emergent misbehavior originated, since the coupled behaviors may never appear together in any single document. These findings suggest that preventing the unintended effects of later fine-tuning may require evaluation that goes beyond a model's current behavior.

items.title: ECG-Reasoning-Benchmark: A Benchmark for Evaluating Clinical Reasoning Capabilities in ECG Interpretation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ECG-Reasoning-Benchmark: A Benchmark for Evaluating Clinical Reasoning Capabilities in ECG Interpretation
items.summary: arXiv:2603.14326v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show promising performance in automated electrocardiogram interpretation, it remains unclear whether they perform actual step-by-step reasoning or just rely on superficial visual cues. To investigate this, we introduce ECG-Reasoning-Benchmark, a novel multi-turn evaluation framework comprising over 6,400 samples to systematically assess step- by-step reasoning across 17 core ECG diagnoses. Our comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art models reveals a systematic shortfall in executing multi-step logical deduction. Although models possess the medical knowledge to retrieve clinical criteria for a diagnosis, they exhibit consistently low success rates in maintaining a complete reasoning chain, primarily failing to ground the corresponding ECG findings to the actual visual evidence in the ECG signal. These results demonstrate that current MLLMs bypass actual visual interpretation, highlighting a limitation in their visual grounding capabilities and motivating robust, reasoning-centric medical AI. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Jwoo5/ecg-reasoning-benchmark.

To investigate this, we introduce ECG-Reasoning-Benchmark, a novel multi-turn evaluation framework comprising over 6,400 samples to systematically assess step- by-step reasoning across 17 core ECG diagnoses. Our comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art models reveals a systematic shortfall in executing multi-step logical deduction. Although models possess the medical knowledge to retrieve clinical criteria for a diagnosis, they exhibit consistently low success rates in maintaining a complete reasoning chain, primarily failing to ground the corresponding ECG findings to the actual visual evidence in the ECG signal. These results demonstrate that current MLLMs bypass actual visual interpretation, highlighting a limitation in their visual grounding capabilities and motivating robust, reasoning-centric medical AI. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Jwoo5/ecg-reasoning-benchmark.

items.title: ROM: Real-time Overthinking Mitigation via Streaming Detection and Intervention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ROM: Real-time Overthinking Mitigation via Streaming Detection and Intervention
items.summary: arXiv:2603.22016v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) often suffer from overthinking, continuing with redundant verification and repeated attempts even after reaching a correct solution. This wastes computation and can overturn an initially correct answer. We show that the transition from productive to redundant reasoning is decodable from late-layer hidden states. These representations separate the two phases around first-correct-solution boundaries beyond what position and lexical controls explain, and distinguish correct from incorrect solution endings. Building on this finding, we propose ROM (Real-time Overthinking Mitigation), which uses a lightweight streaming detector (0.07--0.25\% of backbone parameters) to monitor a frozen LRM and intervene at well-formed reasoning boundaries without answer extraction or probe decoding. Counterfactual Self-Correction (CSC) augments detector training with wrong$\rightarrow$correct trajectories to preserve useful self-correction. Heads are trained separately for each backbone using shared MATH500 supervision and transfer zero-shot to four unseen benchmarks. Evaluated against ten baselines across five backbones from three families and five benchmarks, ROM$_{\text{CSC}}$ reduces response length by 28--77\% (45\% on average), with significant reductions in all 25 settings and accuracy matching or exceeding vanilla decoding in 22. Measurements on two backbones further show 20--70\% lower end-to-end latency with less than 0.5\% detector overhead per decoding step. Code is available at https://github.com/SaFo-Lab/ROM.

items.title: Learning Mental Models From Unreliable Evidence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning Mental Models From Unreliable Evidence
items.summary: arXiv:2605.24528v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Children expertly construct mental models under uncertainty despite limited world knowledge. Which computational principles make this possible? We study this question in an interactive physical Box Task in which participants infer a latent cause through interaction with a stochastic and partially observed environment. The Box Task was originally designed to study children's puzzle-solving qualitatively. We contribute a computational analysis of behavior that formalizes the cognitive process by which children generate new hypotheses and respond to environmental uncertainty as inference unfolds. Our modeling framework is based on Bayesian particle-based inference, which maintains a small set of working hypotheses and continually generates new ones. We give two complementary implementations of hypothesis representations within this framework: (1) as constraints on evidence, and (2) as executable programs evaluated against evidence. Using the constraint-based formulation, we show that the model needs to account both for subjective reliability of evidence and online hypothesis generation to explain key signatures of children's behavior. Using the programmatic formulation, we show that hypotheses may take the form of partial compositional rules to guide information gathering when evidence interpretation is hard. The programmatic hypotheses are implemented using LLM-based program synthesis, evaluated across three prompt variants and several LLM backends, demonstrating robustness of our approach. Together, these results extend current models of children's inference to account for subjective reliability of evidence and open-ended hypothesis spaces, and provide a computational analysis of the form generated hypotheses may take in practice.

items.title: Forget Attention: Importance-Aware Attention Is All You Need [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Forget Attention: Importance-Aware Attention Is All You Need
items.summary: arXiv:2606.02332v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Attention retrieves content precisely, but its scores depend only on query--key products, leaving order and recency to positional encodings. Conversely, state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba-3 track order and recency through input-dependent state transitions that decay and rotate, yet compressing context into a fixed-size state hampers precise retrieval. Hybrids like Samba and Hymba exploit this complementarity only across layers or heads, so SSM transitions never shape attention scores directly. The closest prior work, the Forgetting Transformer (FoX), adds an input-dependent forget gate to the scores but reweights attention by recency alone. We propose SSM-Informed Softmax Attention (SISA), which builds Mamba-3-style state transitions, rotation included, directly into the scores alongside FoX's gate. Each logit receives the weight such an SSM would give that token pair: a decayed match between rotated SSM projections. This rotation already encodes relative position, so SISA drops RoPE; restoring it raises loss. SISA outperforms parameter-matched Transformer and FoX in language modeling and length extrapolation. Among the attention models we compare, hybrids included, only SISA benefits from context beyond the training window. Building SSM transitions into the scores yields stronger attention, and our kernels make it faster and leaner than baselines on their official or standard kernels.

items.title: Interpretability Is Not Just a Tax: Sparsity and Diversity Yield Legible and Composable Reward Experts for Personalization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Interpretability Is Not Just a Tax: Sparsity and Diversity Yield Legible and Composable Reward Experts for Personalization
items.summary: arXiv:2606.04284v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Preference modeling aims to capture heterogeneous human values and increasingly relies on learning latent components to represent this variation without fine-grained supervision. What these components actually represent, however, is rarely examined. We audit Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reward models along three rungs---semantic coherence, functional correspondence, and composability---in controlled and real-world settings, holding the architecture and training data fixed so that differences isolate the effect of the training objective. Our diagnosis is that the components conventional MoE reward models learn are entangled, which limits not only interpretability but also the personalization such models are built for. The entanglement is not intrinsic to the architecture but a property of the training objective: off-the-shelf sparsity and diversity regularizers already substantially reduce it. The resulting configuration, which we call sparse MoE, recovers all underlying semantic categories without domain supervision in a controlled setting, reaching 84.8% expert purity against 60.8% for conventional MoE; on real-world data its experts admit human-interpretable task- and domain-level descriptions aligned with their functional strengths. Targeted interventions on routing weights produce predictable preference changes, showing that these interpretations are behaviorally grounded rather than merely descriptive. Crucially, the disentanglement induced by this objective also makes the experts composable: lightweight router updates yield a 25.81-point improvement in few-shot personalization with 50 examples, roughly 2.7 times the gain of the identical architecture and adaptation procedure applied to entangled experts. Together, these results show that MoE reward models can learn interpretable expert structure, and that the same structure can substantially improve personalization.

items.title: Fine-tuning Multi-modal LLMs with ART: Art-based Reinforcement Training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Fine-tuning Multi-modal LLMs with ART: Art-based Reinforcement Training
items.summary: arXiv:2606.11854v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to specific tasks usually involves fine-tuning: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) edits the weights, while soft prompting prepends trainable virtual tokens. Both change how an already-optimized model is served, so serving many task-specific adapters at high throughput requires adapter-aware infrastructure. We propose Art-Based Reinforcement Training (ART), which optimizes a single auxiliary input image to specialize a frozen Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) for a specific task. At inference time, ART simply includes this image in each standard multimodal prompt, requiring no changes to the serving engine. We compare ART with LoRA and soft prompting across five reasoning benchmarks for four small MLLMs from three architectures. While different methods perform best for different tasks, ART ranks first or second in 10 of 20 benchmark-MLLM pairs, with its best results on the two math word problem benchmarks (GSM8k and SVAMP). It is significantly ahead of the next best adapter in 2 cases, within the noise of the next best adapter in 6, and significantly above the text-only baseline in 18. ART therefore reaches accuracy close to LoRA and soft prompts while serving faster than LoRA. In the vLLM serving stack, ART reduces throughput by 6% to 14% relative to text-only requests, compared to LoRA's 13% to 93% slowdown. Beyond efficient serving, ART artifacts are plain images, making them easy to store, distribute, and share. This approach keep task-specific adaptation outside the model weights, so the same frozen model can support different tasks without separate model variants.

items.title: Reinforcement learning to improve large language model-based automated code compliance systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Reinforcement learning to improve large language model-based automated code compliance systems
items.summary: arXiv:2606.22402v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based approaches for automated code compliance (ACC) of building regulations are prone to generating incorrect and hallucinated computer-processable rules. This paper introduces P4IR, a two-stage framework that uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to instill domain knowledge in an LLM, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to improve the accuracy of the generated intermediate representations in the form of high-level code skeletons. The framework achieved final reductions of up to 21.3% and 41.0% in tree edit distance and token-level Levenshtein distance respectively, relative to the SFT baselines. Comparative analysis demonstrates that this approach in a zero-shot setting outperforms leading LLMs in both code structure and semantics, evaluated via few-shot prompting. Additionally, the GRPO stage produced a statistically significant reduction in false positives. By combining SFT with GRPO to optimize directly for domain-specific objectives, this approach offers a path toward more accurate and reliable LLM-based ACC systems.

items.title: Wiring Beats Blending: Structure-Aware Compensation for Transformer Downscaling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Wiring Beats Blending: Structure-Aware Compensation for Transformer Downscaling
items.summary: arXiv:2608.02829v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model families are trained size by size. Can a pretrained large model instead be converted into a smaller sibling? We characterize the 1.4B->410M conversion in Pythia end to end. Representations align strongly across sizes (ridge R^2=0.84); parameters align weakly. Dense weight projection is destructive; a bit-exact control places the fault in basis mixing, which breaks rotary, per-head, GELU, and LayerNorm structure. Residuals after the best-fit linear operator carry no learnable or transferable signal under shuffle controls, so conversion value lives in initialization. Matched-budget continued pre-training separates two independent levers, least-squares compensation (function lever, best zero-shot) and variance-preserving rescale (dynamics lever, best endpoints), with a placement rule read off the architecture: compensation is well-posed exactly where no normalization sits between cut and read; norm-fronted paths take rescale. At 30M tokens compensation beats the best subcloning variant on a width-reduced pair (84.6+-2.1 vs. 90.7+-3.8, 6/6 seeds) and a held-out depth-reduced pair (109.3 vs. 117.9, 3/3 seeds); the two reach parity at 33x the budget, and at ~5x the donor scale the levers anti-synergize. A second family, Qwen3-1.7B->0.6B (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, grouped-query attention), takes the placement rule unchanged but reverses a 2x2 crossing the re-fit with the activation statistic it reads: on Pythia the re-fit carries the gain and the statistic adds 2.3 perplexity; on Qwen3, with far more heterogeneous MLP unit energies, the statistic carries 66 points and the re-fit is a null on top. Informed selection + compensation + rescale is the best arm in both families, 19x and 23x lower perplexity than from scratch at matched budget (2.94 and 3.13 nats), and beats structured pruning plus distillation. Code, checkpoints, and the frozen eval corpus are released.

items.title: The Direction of Ignorance: LLMs Encode and Temper a Unigram Prior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Direction of Ignorance: LLMs Encode and Temper a Unigram Prior
items.summary: arXiv:2609.02959v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: What does a language model predict when it has few clues?The answer lies in its unembedding geometry: a single direction of the unembedding matrix encodes the unigram distribution of the training corpus, which serves as the Bayesian prior the model falls back on when uncertain. This structure, termed the direction of ignorance, appears across all model families examined (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, and Pythia), ranging from 0.4B to 405B parameters. Projecting the final prediction state onto this direction yields a per-token prior loading factor $\lambda$, which declines steadily as the context becomes more informative. Formally, the same projection decomposes the prediction state into two orthogonal vectors interpretable as the two components of a tempered Bayesian update: a unigram prior raised to the exponent $\lambda$ and a context-driven likelihood. This geometric probabilistic connection makes $\lambda$ meaningfully comparable across model sizes and families. Larger models generally exhibit lower prior reliance, and reasoning models exhibit lower reliance than their base counterparts. Finally, we show that $\lambda$ serves as a causal, inference-time control: reducing it can promote context-driven continuations and improve Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on GSM8K, whereas amplifying it or applying matched perturbations along random directions degrades performance.

items.title: The Best Second Opinion Is Right Where the Primary Is Wrong: Partner Selection for Selective Span Tagging [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Best Second Opinion Is Right Where the Primary Is Wrong: Partner Selection for Selective Span Tagging
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A span tagger that ranks its outputs by risk can defer the riskiest ones to a person, and a second model can sharpen this ranking. Which second model should it be? Partner selection is conditional, not global: the best second opinion is the model that is right where the primary is wrong. Across eight tagger types, three seeds and three English benchmarks (576 evaluated primary-partner pairings), choosing the partner by held-out accuracy on the primary's errors recovers 82% of the best partner's gain, against 69-70% for span F1 or a random pick. Frozen before a fourth dataset was chosen, the rule replicated there (Spearman 0.40 vs. 0.04 for span F1). Partner value is also directional. The predictive distribution is the second opinion: hard labels discard half of a partner's value, and scoring the served label improves 94% of pairings. Fixed before the fourth dataset was chosen, this score also replicated there. For LoRA-tuned decoders, independently trained partners beat every readout of the primary network. Applied zero-shot to 51 MASSIVE locales, every primary has a helpful trained partner in every locale, and the preferred partner follows competence.

items.title: Exposure Is Not Commitment: Double-Stratified Evaluation of Latent Monitors for Tool-Using Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Exposure Is Not Commitment: Double-Stratified Evaluation of Latent Monitors for Tool-Using Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using language agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, and a growing literature probes model internals to catch unsafe actions before they execute, with sharply conflicting results. We argue much of the conflict is an evaluation artifact, and propose a double-stratification protocol: separate injection exposure from behavioral commitment, in both the evaluation and the training population. On the primary Qwen AgentDojo grid, monitors trained on the naive mixed unsafe-versus-rest contrast mostly learn exposure: they flag exposed trajectories whether or not the agent complies, and barely predict which cases turn unsafe. Retrained on exposed cases only, the same probe families predict the model's own unsafe tool call up to two steps early, the maximum the three-step trajectories admit (logistic AUROC 0.853, matched by a trained TF-IDF text baseline at 0.855). Mistral-7B reaches 0.896 and OLMo-2-7B 0.912; their naive contrasts learn different things: inverted exposure ranking on one, both axes on the other. Representations separate on exposure (probe 1.000 versus trained text 0.908) and where visible context is sanitized or unavailable. Training contrast alone reproduces the shape of recent pre-action-probe negative results, one candidate explanation for the conflict: the signal exists, but the model's own zero-shot forecast and NLA verbalizations do not reliably recover it. An unstratified AUROC overstates what a latent monitor knows, and what a naive contrast learns is population-dependent: evaluations should stratify both.
